aAbout: EarthCam runs a network of live webcams anchored by famous places — Times Square in New York is the signature view — organised into destination pages and EarthCam TV channels that package cameras into themed streams. Alongside the free consumer network it sells professional construction-camera systems to businesses, with managed hardware, archiving and time-lapse. Many public cameras are watchable free in the browser and in its mobile apps, with weather information shown alongside some cameras.
aStrengths: EarthCam is the deeper platform for famous places: a large, long-running network of scenic and tourist cameras anchored by Times Square, curated viewing through EarthCam TV, and professional construction-camera services with managed hardware, archiving and time-lapse for commercial clients. For watching a specific famous place — or for a business that needs a camera installed and managed — EarthCam's camera-specific depth and history beat a satellite map, which can never show you the street-level scene at all.
bAbout: Zoom Earth is an interactive weather map and real-time hurricane tracker by Neave Interactive. It shows near real-time satellite imagery updated every 10 minutes from NOAA GOES, JMA Himawari and EUMETSAT Meteosat geostationary satellites, HD imagery updated twice a day from NASA's Aqua and Terra satellites, rain radar with nowcasting, and forecast maps for rain, wind, temperature, pressure and more from the ICON and GFS models. It runs free on the web and in iOS and Android apps, with extra features behind Zoom Earth Pro. It is a weather and satellite tool — not a camera network, and it does not track flights or ships.
bStrengths: Zoom Earth is the deeper weather tool by a wide margin: satellite imagery refreshed every 10 minutes, rain radar with nowcasting, a best-in-class hurricane tracker drawing on NHC, JTWC, NRL and IBTrACS data, wildfire heat spots from NASA FIRMS, and a full set of forecast-model maps — all in a clean, focused interface that opens instantly on the web or in its well-rated mobile apps, with no account needed for basic use. If the question is about a storm, Zoom Earth answers it faster and in more depth.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. EarthCam is a dedicated webcam network built for watching places: famous landmark cameras and TV-style channels, free to open, with a professional camera business alongside. Zoom Earth is a hosted weather specialist: near real-time satellite imagery, radar and hurricane tracking that open instantly in a browser or app, with no ground cameras at all. If you want to *see the place*, open EarthCam; if you want to *see the weather over the place*, open Zoom Earth.

intro: EarthCam and Zoom Earth both show you the planet live — from opposite directions. EarthCam looks along the ground: a long-running network of live webcams anchored by famous places, Times Square above all, organised into destination pages and EarthCam TV channels. Zoom Earth looks down from orbit: an interactive weather map by Neave Interactive with satellite imagery updated every 10 minutes, rain radar with nowcasting and a hurricane tracker. One answers 'what does the place look like right now?'; the other answers 'what is the weather doing over the place right now?'
pricingA: Watching EarthCam's public cameras is free. Its professional construction-camera services, hardware and business offerings are paid and typically quoted per project — there is no consumer subscription comparable to a premium tier.
pricingB: Zoom Earth is free for basic use on the web and in its iOS and Android apps, with no account required. Zoom Earth Pro adds more features through auto-renewable subscriptions sold via the app stores: the US App Store listing shows Pro price points of $1.99 and $11.99, but it does not label which billing period each price corresponds to, so we won't assign one — its terms say subscriptions are billed periodically, as specified at the time of purchase. No free trial of Pro was stated on the official pages checked.

verdictA: Choose EarthCam if you want to see the place itself — famous landmark views like Times Square, curated TV-style channels, or professional construction-camera services for a business site — and you want to just open a browser or an app and watch.
verdictB: Choose Zoom Earth if you want to see the weather over the place — 10-minute satellite imagery, radar, forecast maps and serious hurricane tracking — open in seconds on any device, with no install.
verdictLine: EarthCam is the ground view — real cameras in real places, built for watching. Zoom Earth is the sky view — satellite imagery and weather maps, built for tracking storms. Neither does the other's job, and many people will honestly want both.
worldEye: If you want the ground view and the sky view in one place, WorldEye puts 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries on a free interactive 3D globe — together with live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. There is nothing to install and no signup: the map is free, and an optional Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds the OSINT toolkit and intel feeds. It will not replace EarthCam's construction services or Zoom Earth's 10-minute satellite cadence and hurricane depth, but it is the one option here that shows a place's cameras and the weather moving over it together.
